content: 1. CASPER (Community Assessments for Public Health Emergency Response) is a public health tool designed to collect household-level information within a community. It is an efficient epidemiologic method that provides emergency planners and responders, such as emergency managers, with quick and cost-effective data. 2. During a CASPER survey, you can ask specific closed-ended questions, such as: What is your primary source of information regarding disaster or emergency events? What factors might prevent you from evacuating if asked to do so? Does your household currently have a 7-day supply of medication for each person taking prescription drugs? 3. Emergency managers can collaborate with public health colleagues to utilize CASPER in all phases of the disaster lifecycle. Public health departments often use CASPER during disaster response to assess immediate needs, such as determining the number of households without access to potable water in the affected area. 4. CASPER is also used during the preparedness phase to aid in planning. For example, it can help identify the number of households in a community that have an emergency preparedness kit. 5. Public health departments can work with emergency managers to determine the optimal timing for conducting a CASPER survey and to design questions that prioritize response efforts and resource distribution. 6. Focus groups are used to uncover attitudes, perceptions, and behaviors of participants, providing an in-depth understanding of at-risk groups in the community. Specific open-ended questions during focus groups may include: What sources do you typically use to get news and information? How do you receive information during a disaster? How do you prefer information to be communicated to you? What barriers have prevented you from receiving critical information in the past? 7. Focus groups are valuable for obtaining feedback on existing public health interventions or for designing new ones. Emergency managers can collaborate with public health departments to plan and conduct focus groups to gather insights on attitudes, perceptions, and behaviors before, during, and after emergencies. 8. Understanding at-risk groups better enhances the ability to reach and assist them effectively. 9. Data collected through surveys and focus groups can help identify cultural and language barriers faced by at-risk individuals in the community. Communication plans must address these barriers to provide clear instructions before, during, and after a disaster. 10. Effective communication strategies include: Using short sentences and plain language for easy translation. Providing written materials in bilingual or multilingual formats. Including visual aids like pictures and maps to reinforce key messages. Repeating critical information. Including clear directions and contact information. Using large fonts for readability. Identifying preferred communication methods (e.g., face-to-face, phone, word-of-mouth) and tailoring messages accordingly. Identifying preferred media channels (e.g., local newspapers, ethnic radio stations, church leaders) for message dissemination. 11. Trusted messengers are crucial for delivering emergency messages to at-risk groups. People are more likely to respond to messages from individuals they perceive as part of their community, such as neighbors, religious leaders, or community leaders. 12. When developing an emergency communication plan, identify appropriate and trusted messengers to deliver information. Trusted sources may include members of your community network, religious leaders, barbers, hairstylists, or ethnic media outlets. 13. The Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) uses U.S. Census and American Community Survey data to identify at-risk groups by ranking census tracts based on social vulnerability factors. These factors are grouped into four main themes. 14. Emergency managers can use the SVI to locate areas with the highest numbers of at-risk individuals. The SVI provides tools and resources to create customized maps and enhance communication plans by including at-risk populations and designating trusted spokespersons. 15. Combining individualand population-level data provides a comprehensive understanding of the needs of at-risk groups in the community. 16. This guidance document equips emergency managers with the tools and strategies needed to develop comprehensive emergency plans that address the unique needs of at-risk groups before, during, and after emergencies.
